lead.text: The Express 'xss' sanitizer middleware (index.js::middleware, an EntryPoint handler) takes attacker-controlled req.body, req.params, req.headers (index.js:7-9: `req[k] = sanitize(req[k], options)`) and req.query (index.js:12: `sanitize(req.query, options)`, a FLOWS_TO self-loop confirming the call's own argument is tainted) and passes them into lib/sanitize.js's recursive `sanitize(options, data, currentDepth)` (resolved via index.js's imported `sanitize` -> lib/sanitize.js's exported `prepareSanitize` -> internal `sanitize`). For object-typed data, that function does `Object.keys(data).forEach((key) => { if (options.allowedKeys.includes(key)) return; ... data[key] = sanitizeHtml(item, options.sanitizerOptions); /* or */ data[key] = sanitize(options, item, currentDepth + 1); })` (lib/sanitize.js:51-60). `key` is taken directly from `Object.keys()` of attacker-supplied data with no denylist anywhere in the codebase for `__proto__`, `constructor`, or `prototype` (confirmed: zero calls/code in the scan reference 'proto' or 'constructor'); the only filter is the dev-configured `allowedKeys` allowlist, which defaults to `[]` and serves an unrelated purpose (skip-sanitizing certain keys), not key-safety. A request body/query/params/headers field literally named `__proto__` (or nested under one) that reaches this per-key dynamic write is a classic CWE-1321 prototype-pollution gadget pattern: `data[key] = <value>` with a fully attacker-controlled `key`. This is the single highest-centrality node in the file (lib/sanitize.js::program:sanitize, centrality 0.01205, the top chokepoint other than initializeOptions), so every sanitized field in every request funnels through this unguarded write. Practical exploitability depends on whether the upstream body/query parser preserves `__proto__` as the object's own shadowing data property (as JSON.parse typically does) or instead triggers the inherited Object.prototype.__proto__ accessor (e.g. headers/params objects built field-by-field, or non-JSON parsers); this caveat should be checked against the real body-parser/qs configuration before confirming, but the sink code itself has no protection regardless of parser behavior.

reason:
I confirmed the code shape the analyst cites is real (read index.js:1-26 and lib/sanitize.js:1-72 directly), and confirmed via mcp__orion__run_cypher that lib/sanitize.js::program:sanitize is reachable_from_entry=true, hop_distance=0, centrality=0.01205 (highest in file, matching the claim), and that index.js::program:middleware is an EntryPoint (kind=handler, exposure=reachable). The sink code `Object.keys(data).forEach(key => { ...; data[key] = sanitizeHtml(item,...) /* or */ data[key] = sanitize(options, item, depth+1) })` (lib/sanitize.js:51-60) genuinely has no __proto__/constructor/prototype denylist, and 'proto'/'constructor' do not appear anywhere in CpgCall.code for this scan (re-ran the analyst's query, 0 rows) -- so the structural claim is accurate.

However, the actual exploitability claim fails on JS/Node semantics I verified against this package's own test file (test/test.js:10-18 shows `bodyParser.urlencoded({extended:true})` + `bodyParser.json()` as the standard config). (1) req.body/req.query parsed via JSON.parse: per the ECMAScript spec, JSON.parse builds objects via CreateDataProperty, which creates `__proto__` as a literal OWN data property shadowing the inherited accessor -- it never invokes the Object.prototype.__proto__ setter. So `data["__proto__"]` in sanitize.js just reads/rewrites that own shadow property; `Object.getPrototypeOf(data)` is never touched and no global pollution occurs. (2) req.query/urlencoded body parsed via `qs` (used here via extended:true): qs has long explicitly special-cased the literal key `__proto__` in its object-building (parseObject) to refuse to set it, independent of the `allowedKeys` option in this package -- so `__proto__` typically never survives into `data` as a key at all via that parser. (3) req.headers: Node always delivers header values as strings (or, only for a small allow-list like set-cookie, arrays of strings -- `__proto__` is not on that list, so repeated headers get comma-joined into a string); the native `__proto__` accessor setter is a no-op whenever the assigned value is not an object or null, so `data['__proto__'] = <string>` in sanitize.js cannot trigger `[[SetPrototypeOf]]`. (4) req.params keys come from the developer's own route-pattern definition, not from attacker input, so an attacker cannot even supply a key named `__proto__` there. Across all four cited vectors, under the parsing configuration this package itself tests with, the single-level `data[key]=value` write cannot reach real Object.prototype pollution despite the missing denylist. No CandidateFlow, runtime hit, or PoC in the scan supports actual exploitation either. This is a real defense-in-depth gap (worth hardening) but not a demonstrated, exploitable CWE-1321 vulnerability as framed by the lead.

lead.text: The express-xss-sanitizer middleware (`xss` exported from index.js) sanitizes req.body, req.params, req.headers, and req.query against XSS payloads, but never includes req.cookies in the sanitized key set. Cookies are a standard attacker-controlled input channel (the task's own source list calls out req.cookies.* alongside body/query/params/headers), and the middleware's entire stated purpose is to neutralize untrusted input before it reaches route handlers/templates. Any downstream handler that reads req.cookies.* (e.g. a cookie-parser-populated object) receives raw, unsanitized attacker-controlled strings, defeating the protection this middleware is supposed to provide for that input vector.

However this is not a security defect in this codebase, it is the library's documented, intentional scope. package.json:4 and README.md:2 both state the library's stated purpose verbatim: "sanitizes user input data (in req.body, req.query, req.headers and req.params)" — cookies are explicitly absent from the library's own advertised contract, so there is no broken promise to 'defeat'. Additionally, the scanned codebase (confirmed via CpgFile query: only index.js and lib/sanitize.js exist) contains no cookie-parser dependency (Dependency query returned 12 deps, none related to cookies), no req.cookies reference anywhere, and no consuming route handler at all — this is a standalone middleware library, not an application. The attack scenario in the claim ("downstream handler that reads req.cookies.*, e.g. a cookie-parser-populated object") is entirely hypothetical and points to code that does not exist anywhere in this scan's scope. There is no concrete reachable sink to confirm exploitability against; the finding amounts to 'this sanitizer doesn't sanitize an input channel it never claimed to sanitize,' which is a scope/feature observation, not a vulnerability in the code under review.
